- When sentiment is strongly negative (e.g., < -0.5) in recent days, model tends to undercorrect — forecast should be adjusted upward to reflect market resilience or reversal.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >80), model often overreacts with continued upward trend — cap the forecast slope or introduce early mean-reversion logic.
- If sentiment turns positive (e.g., > 0.3) mid-horizon, model frequently fails to catch momentum — increase forecast slope or add sentiment-weighted acceleration.
- Model consistently underestimates true price peaks in 30-day horizon — apply a 5–10% upward bias for high-sentiment periods.
- When sentiment is volatile or mixed (e.g., alternating +/– 0.3), model over-smooths — introduce stochastic or adaptive smoothing to capture sentiment-driven volatility.
- Forecast often lags true price by 2–3 days in upward moves — adjust for 1–2 day lead-in if sentiment is bullish.
- If true outcome shows early mean reversion (e.g., peak then drop), model tends to over-forecast later peaks — reduce forecast slope after peak or add decay factor.
